opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've had to update on a lot. Before working at a big lab, I had a fairly naive model where an organisation is like a single agent: there's some leadership with goals, they make decisions, and those decisions get carried out. If you wanted to change what the organisation does, you'd make a good argument to the right person and that would be that.

The reality is much messier, and honestly more interesting. A large organisation is really a lot of people with their own incentives, priorities, and limited attention, all trying to coordinate. Most decisions aren't made in one dramatic meeting. They come out of a ton of smaller choices: what gets resourced, which teams talk to each other, what's legible to senior people, what someone happened to raise at the right moment. A lot of what looks like a deliberate strategy from outside is closer to the emergent result of many local decisions.

A few things stand out to me. First, attention is incredibly scarce. Senior people are juggling an enormous number of things, so an idea being *correct* isn't enough. It needs to be clearly expressed, tied to things they already care about, and arrive when there's a decision it can actually affect. I've seen great ideas go nowhere because nobody was positioned to act on them, and fairly mundane ideas have real impact because they landed at the right time.

Second, trust and relationships matter much more than I expected. If people know you, think you're reasonable, and have seen you deliver, they're far more willing to take your concerns seriously. That's partly why I think people who want to influence how AI gets developed often underrate just being a competent, trusted colleague doing good work inside the org. That credibility is what lets you push back when it really matters.

Third, I've become much more sympathetic to people making decisions under constraints I can't see. From the outside it's easy to think "why don't they just do the obvious thing?" Often there are legal, commercial, or coordination considerations that make the obvious thing much harder than it looks. That doesn't mean organisations always get it right, far from it, but I've become more cautious about assuming bad faith when inertia or competing priorities explain things better.

So the practical takeaway for me is: if you want to change an organisation's behaviour, think less about winning an argument and more about who decides what, what they're optimising for, what information they actually see, and how to make the good option the easy option. That's less glamorous, but it's usually how things actually change.

r001.rationale: The response calls the single-agent model naive and describes large organisations as many people coordinating through local decisions.

r002.rationale: It says people have their own incentives and priorities, indicating that different stakeholders bring different interests to the organisation.

r003.rationale: The response mentions senior people and competing priorities, but does not say that disagreement causes decisions to escalate to more senior decision-makers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest update I had from actually working inside large organisations is that the mental model of "an organisation is an agent that makes decisions" is just wrong, and it's wrong in ways that really matter if you're trying to predict what a company will do or trying to change it.

Before I'd worked anywhere serious, I think I implicitly modelled companies like Google or DeepMind as having a kind of unified will. Like, "Google decided X" or "the lab believes Y". And the reality is much messier and much more mundane. An organisation is a very large number of people, each of whom has their own incentives, their own local information, their own sense of what they're being evaluated on, and mostly fairly limited visibility into what everyone else is doing. The "decision" that comes out the other end is often less a decision than an emergent outcome of a lot of people each doing the thing that made sense from where they were standing.

A few things that fell out of that for me. One is that the amount of explicit coordination is much lower than you'd expect. There's no room where someone has the full picture and is weighing everything up. Even very senior people are operating on compressed summaries that have passed through several layers, and a lot of nuance gets lost at each layer. So if you're a researcher who thinks "surely leadership knows about this problem", the honest answer is often: maybe, maybe not, and even if they do, they know a two-sentence version of it.

Another is that momentum and defaults are incredibly powerful. A lot of what happens in a big organisation is just whatever was already happening, continuing. Changing direction requires someone to spend political capital, write a doc, convince people, get resources reallocated. So the default path has a huge advantage, and if you want to steer things, a lot of the work is about making your preferred option the easy option rather than winning an argument on the merits.

And a third, which I think is actually a fairly hopeful lesson, is that individual people can have way more influence than the "faceless corporation" framing suggests. Because things are undetermined and nobody has the full picture, a motivated person who writes the clear doc, builds the relationships, and shows up in the right meetings can genuinely shift what happens. Lots of what look from the outside like big institutional choices were really one or two people pushing for something and not getting enough pushback. That cuts both ways, obviously, but it does mean that if you care about something like safety, being inside and being competent and being persistent matters a lot.

The flip side is I've become a lot more sceptical of narratives that attribute coherent strategic intent to organisations. When someone says "the lab is doing this because they secretly want that", my prior is now that it's much more likely to be some combination of inertia, a particular team's incentives, and nobody having quite thought it through, than a master plan. Which is less satisfying as a story, but I think it's more accurate, and it changes what the useful interventions actually look like.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly rejects the idea that an organisation has a unified will or acts as a single agent making decisions.

r002.rationale: It says people have their own incentives and local information, but does not clearly explain that stakeholders represent different interests important to the organisation.

r003.rationale: It describes information passing through senior layers, but does not identify disagreement as a reason decisions escalate to senior decision-makers.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest update is that an organisation is much less of a single coherent agent than it looks from the outside. You see a company do something and think, “Why did they decide that?” But there may not be a single person who decided it in the sense you’re imagining. There are different teams with different priorities, people with incomplete information, and decisions that happen because someone pushed for something and nobody else felt strongly enough to stop it.

That doesn’t mean everyone is irrational. You can have individually sensible people, each responding reasonably to their own constraints, and still get a result that looks pretty strange overall. Even just getting the relevant information to the person who can act on it is a substantial problem.

So I’m more sceptical of explanations that assume a company has one clear goal and is executing a carefully thought-out strategy. I’d want to ask: who actually has authority here? What do they know? What are they incentivised to do? And who cares enough to make this happen? Those questions seem much more useful for understanding a particular decision.

r001.rationale: The response questions explanations that assume a company has one clear goal and describes decisions arising from people and teams with different priorities.

r002.rationale: It says different teams have different priorities and people face different constraints, communicating that organisational stakeholders can bring distinct interests.

r003.rationale: The response mentions differing priorities and who has authority, but does not say disagreement causes decisions to escalate to more senior decision-makers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think working in a real company made me much less inclined to think of an organisation as a single coherent agent. From the outside, you see a decision and ask, “Why did the company want that?” From the inside, there are a bunch of people with different information, different priorities, and different constraints, trying to get something done.

A lot of what looks like a deliberate choice is actually the default outcome of nobody having the time, context, or authority to change it. And something that seems obviously sensible to one team can create a lot of work for another team, so it just doesn’t happen.

That’s made me more interested in the actual mechanism: who can make this decision? What do they believe? What are they rewarded for? Who would need to agree? I think those questions are usually much more useful than asking what “the organisation” thinks.

r001.rationale: It says an organisation is not a single coherent agent and describes decisions as emerging from people with differing information, priorities, and constraints.

r002.rationale: It explains that people and teams have different priorities and constraints, including cases where what suits one team burdens another.

r003.rationale: It does not say that disagreement causes decisions to escalate to more senior decision-makers.
